Learning Objectives
Describe risk factors for and the pathoanatomy of closed space infections of the hand and
wrist, including fingertip infections, septic arthritis, and pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis.
Discuss the nonsurgical versus surgical treatment of patients with a hand and wrist infection
with appropriate urgency.
Review treatment options for patients with a hand and wrist infection, including indications for
surgical treatment.
Describe the clinical presentation of, diagnostic studies for, and treatment steps for
necrotizing fasciitis.
Explain the clinical presentation and differentiating factors associated with atypical hand and
wrist infections and mimickers of hand and wrist infections.

Paronychia
Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Paronychia are infections of the soft tissues surrounding the nail plate.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of paronychia.

Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Paronychia are infections of the soft tissues about the nail plate (eponychium,
paronychium, and hyponychium) and typically manifest in the proximal and/or lateral
fingernail folds. Paronychia may occur spontaneously or may be associated with local
trauma or skin irritation. These infections may occur in patients who commonly place
their hands in water (eg, cleaners) or patients who sustain local skin trauma (e.g.,
manicures, nail biting).1 The most common causative microorganism is S aureus;
however, but Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas pyocyanea, Proteus vulgaris, Eikenella
corrodens, and Klebsiella pneumoniae have been implicated.1, 2
Clinical Presentation/Diagnosis
Acute paronychia present with as tenderness, swelling, and erythema of the proximal and/or
lateral nail folds.
Radiographs can may be consideredobtained; however, theybut may be appear normal,
except for dorsal soft- tissue swelling in the region about the nail fold region.

Clinical Presentation/Diagnosis
Acute paronychia present as pain, tenderness, swelling, and erythema of the proximal
and/or lateral nail folds. Patients with more advanced paronychia may present with
collections of purulence in the nail folds or beneath the nail plate.2

Management
Acute paronychia without an abscess are managed with via oral antibiotic therapy, with or
without soaks.
Acute paronychia with an abscess are treated managed viawith incision and drainage of the
affected region of the nail fold, including removal of part or all of the nail plate.

Management
Acute paronychia without purulent collection are managed via oral antibiotic therapy
with or without intermittent warm saline soaks. Oral cephalexin, clindamycin,
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or amoxicillin in combination with clavulanate are
common antibiotic treatment options that are effective against the most common
causative microorganisms.2 No comparative trials on these antibiotic agents have been
performed; however, clindamycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be
considered in communities with a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant S aureus.3 In
theory, warm compresses or soaks may improve spontaneous drainage of occult
purulence; however, high-level evidence has not demonstrated their efficacy.4
Incision and drainage of the acute paronychia is indicated in patients with an abscess.
This may involve incision of the nail fold or removal of part or all the nail plate,
particularly if the abscess is subungual. Oral antibiotic agents, packing, and/or soaks are
appropriate.2
Chronic Paronychia
Chronic paronychia may present as induration, drainage, and nail plate changes.
Nonsurgical management includes topical gentian violet dye treatment.
Surgical management may necessitate nail plate removal and eponychial marsupialization.

Chronic Paronychia
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000665
3/38

Chronic paronychia may represent long-term infection versus a prolonged inflammatory
response after acute infection. Patients with chronic paronychia present with less
erythema but have skin induration, rounding of the eponychium, recurrent drainage,
and nail plate thickness and deformity.3 Chronic paronychia may be managed
nonsurgically via reassurance and observation. Treatment Management via topical
gentian violet dye also is recommended. Surgical management involves described is nail
plate removal and eponychial marsupialization, in which a crescent of skin parallel to the
eponychium is excised and the wound allowed to heal via secondary intention. This
procedure is followed by dressing changes, soaks, and oral antibiotic therapy.5 Surgical
management should be carefully considered. Many hand surgeons do not perform this
procedure and, instead, favor reassurance and observation.
Felon
Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Felons are infections of the volar digital pulp.
Neglected felons may cause pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis or osteomyelitis.
S aureus is the most common organism associated with felon.

Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Felons are infections of the volar pulp of the digit. The anatomy of the digital pulp
consists of fibrous septae from the periosteum to the skin. The buildup of purulent
collections in these septated compartments may cause considerable pain.6 These
septated compartments of the volar pulp are believed to act as small, closed spaces in
which infection may be loculated (Figure 1) . Neglected felons may lead to pyogenic
flexor tenosynovitis or osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx. The most common causative
microorganism is S aureus.7, 8

Figure 1
Sagittal (A) and cross-sectional (B) view illustrations of the fingertip show the fibrous,
septated compartments of the pulp. (Reproduced from Adams JE: Fingertip infections, in
Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 477-480.)
Clinical Presentation/Diagnosis
Patients with an acute felon present with pain, tenderness, and swelling of the volar digital
pulp.
Radiographs should be obtained to assess for osteomyelitis and foreign bodies.

Clinical Presentation/Diagnosis
Patients with an acute felon present with pain, tenderness, and swelling at the volar
digital pulp because of the buildup of purulence in septated compartments of the pulp.6,
7 A physical examination should be performed to determine if tenderness, swelling, or
erythema is present more proximally along the digit, such as along the flexor tendon
sheath. Radiographs can be obtained to assess for osteomyelitis and in patients with
penetrating trauma, to assess for foreign bodies.7
Management

Patients who have a mild acute felon without clear loculated purulence of the digital pulp or
radiographic abnormalities are treated via oral antibiotic therapy, with or without soaks.
Patients who have an acute felon with tenseness of the digital pulp concerning for abscess
require incision and drainage of the purulent collections in the digital pulp, ensuring any
intervening septae are disrupted.

Management
Early felons without abscess formation may be managed via oral antibiotic therapy with
or without intermittent warm saline soaks. Felons with abscess formation are managed
via incision and drainage of the purulent collections in the digital pulp. If possible,
incision on the ulnar side of the ring and little digits and incision on the radial side of the
index and long digits should be avoided. Surgeons should spread through the incision
with the use of a blunt instrument to disrupt intervening septae, which ensures that the
felon is adequately drained and decompressed6, 7(Figure 2).
Figure 2
Illustrations of the fingertip show a central longitudinal incision (A) and a midaxial incision (B) for
drainage of a felon. Typically, the area of most fluctuance is incised and drained. Care should be
taken if using the incision shown in panel B (or similar incisions) because it may be associated
with increased scar sensitivity or decreased sensation of the digit if the incision or dissection

Septic Arthritis
Pathoanatomy / Microbiology
Septic arthritis are closed space infections of the joints, accounting for 8% to 27% of all
patients who present with an acutely painful and swollen joint.
S aureus and beta-hemolytic Streptococcus are the most common causes of septic arthritis.
A high suspicion for metacarpophalangeal joint septic arthritis should be maintained in
patients with a fight bite.

Pathoanatomy / Microbiology
Acute bacterial septic arthritis is a closed space infection of a joint, such as an
interphalangeal joint, a metacarpophalangeal joint, or the wrist joint. Based on two prior
prospective studies, septic arthritis accounts for 8% to 27% of all patients who present to
an emergency department with an acutely painful and swollen joint.9, 10 Articular
cartilage damage can occur via the release of bacterial toxins and the local inflammatory
response.
Septic arthritis can result from hematologic spread. The differential diagnosis frequently
includes crystalline arthropathy and inflammatory arthritis6 (Table 1). The most common
causative microorganisms are S aureus and beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. Neisseria
gonorrhoeae should be considered in patients who are sexually active.8, 11
Another common cause of septic arthritis in the hand is direct inoculation, such as into
the metacarpophalangeal joint via a fight bite. Contact of a clenched fist with a human
tooth can injure the extensor tendon, dorsal joint capsule, and metacarpal head articular
cartilage and seed the joint with bacteria. Although various causative microorganisms

common.8

Clinical Presentation
Septic arthritis presents as joint swelling, erythema, and pain with active and passive joint
motion.
Patients may present with systemic symptoms, such as a fever.

Clinical Presentation
A meta-analysis of 14 studies, which included 653 patients with septic arthritis out of a
total cohort of 6,242 patients, reported that joint pain (85% sensitivity), joint swelling
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000665
8/38

(78% sensitivity), and fever (57% sensitivity) were reported in more than one-half of
patients with septic arthritis. The constitutional symptoms of sweating (27% sensitivity)
and rigor (19% sensitivity) were less diagnostically useful.12
Diagnostic Studies
Radiographs are helpful because many arthropathies are included in the differential diagnosis.
A serum white blood cell (WBC) count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein
(CRP) level, and blood cultures are appropriate.
Synovial fluid analysis should include a Gram stain, cultures, a WBC count with differential, and
polarized light microscopy for crystal analysis.
A synovial fluid WBC count higher than 50,000 cells/μL with more than 75%
polymorphonuclear leukocytes is diagnostic for septic arthritis.
If limited joint fluid is available for analysis, a Gram stain, cultures, and crystal analysis should
be prioritized over cell count.

Diagnostic Studies
Serum laboratory studies, including a WBC count with differential, ESR, and CRP level,
are appropriate if concern for septic arthritis exists. An elevated WBC count is commonly
higher than 10,000 cells/μL, an elevated ESR is commonly higher than 30 mm/h, and an
elevated CRP level is commonly higher than 100 mg/L.12
Synovial fluid aspiration provides useful diagnostic information; however, it may be
technically challenging to perform in the small joints of the hand or if fluid in the wrist
joint is insufficient.6 If synovial fluid can be obtained, analysis should include a Gram
stain, cultures, a WBC count with differential, and polarized light microscopy for crystal
analysis.11 A synovial fluid WBC count higher than 50,000 cells/μL and with more than
75% polymorphonuclear leukocytes has historically been used as the threshold for septic
arthritis.8, 11 A retrospective study of 156 patients who underwent arthrocentesis, 10%
of whom had septic arthritis, suggested that a synovial fluid WBC cutoff value of 17,500
cells/μL optimizes the sensitivity (83%) and specificity (67%) of the diagnosis of septic

arthritis.13 In the extremely common scenario in which limited joint fluid is available for
analysis, a Gram stain, cultures, and crystal analysis should be prioritized over cell
count.14
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Broad spectrum antibiotic therapy should be initiated and subsequently narrowed and
tailored based on culture data.
Serial needle aspiration may be considered in patients who are poor candidates for surgical
treatment.

Nonsurgical Management
Ideally, antibiotic therapy is initiated after synovial fluid is obtained for analysis if
concern for septic arthritis exists. Broad spectrum intravenous antibiotic agents with
coverage for gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms typically are selected.
These agents can be subsequently narrowed and tailored based on speciation and
sensitivities determined via culture data.11
After a diagnosis of acute bacterial septic arthritis is established, surgical management
generally is performed; however, serial needle aspiration or joint lavage may be
considered in patients who are poor candidates for surgery.15, 16
Surgical Management
Surgical wound irrigation is indicated after a diagnosis of septic arthritis is established to
prevent additional articular damage.
The wrist joint may be effectively drained via an open or arthroscopic approach.
The metacarpophalangeal joints may be approached dorsally, with preservation or incision
and repair of the sagittal bands.

The interphalangeal joints may be drained via a dorsal or midaxial approach.
An alternative treatment option is serial aspiration or joint lavage, which may be helpful in
patients who are poor candidates for surgery.

Surgical Management
After a diagnosis of acute bacterial septic arthritis is established, surgical incision and
drainage of the affected joint and antibiotic therapy are indicated.6, 8, 11 Surgical
management of septic wrist joints can be effectively performed via an open approach
(dorsal approach between the third and fourth extensor tendon compartments) or an
arthroscopic approach.17 The metacarpophalangeal joints may be approached dorsally,
either by splitting the extensor apparatus or by incising the sagittal band with later
repair. The interphalangeal joints may be drained via a midaxial approach or a dorsal
approach (adjacent to the terminal tendon).8
Pyogenic Flexor Tenosynovitis
Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis is a closed space infection of the flexor tendon sheath.
Delayed management of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis may lead to necrosis of the flexor
tendons and the pulley system.
S aureus and beta-hemolytic Streptococcus are the most common causes of pyogenic flexor
tenosynovitis.

Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Acute pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis is a closed space bacterial infection of the flexor
tendon sheath. Purulence in this enclosed space may create pressure that inhibits
perfusion of the tendons, leading to necrosis. The infection also can break down the
retinacular pulley system, causing subcutaneous purulence. In the thumb and little
finger, connections of the radial and ulnar bursae with the Parona space in the wrist may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000665
11/38

lead to contiguous spread of the infection, causing a horseshoe abscess. S aureus and
beta-hemolytic Streptococcus are the most common causes of pyogenic flexor
tenosynovitis.6, 8
Clinical Presentation
The four classic Kanavel signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis are fusiform digital swelling,
pain with passive digital extension, flexed posture of the digit, and tenderness along the flexor
tendon sheath.
Some patients may present with a fever.

Clinical Presentation
The four classic Kanavel signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis are fusiform digital
swelling, pain with passive digital extension, flexed posture of the digit, and tenderness
along the flexor tendon sheath. A retrospective study of 75 patients with pyogenic flexor
tenosynovitis over a 6-year period showed that 97% of the patients had fusiform
swelling, 72% of the patients had pain on passive digital extension, 69% of the patients
had flexed posture of the digit, and 64% of the patients had tenderness along the flexor
tendon sheath.18 All four Kanavel signs may be observed in only 54% of patients with
pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis19 (Figure 3). Fever is a relatively uncommon symptom,
observed in 17% of patients with pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis.18

Diagnostic Studies
Radiographs; serum WBC count, ESR, and CRP level; and blood cultures are appropriate
diagnostic studies.
Management
Nonsurgical Management

13/38

A trial of antibiotic therapy alone may be considered in patients with early flexor tenosynovitis
(approximately ≤24 hours of symptoms) and mild symptoms.
Nonsurgical management consists of broad-spectrum antibiotic agents and serial physical
examinations to ensure clinical improvement.
Elevation to improve edema and splint immobilization for soft-tissue rest are common adjunct
therapies.

Nonsurgical Management
Initial antibiotic treatment should include broad-spectrum antibiotic agents that are
subsequently narrowed based on clinical improvement, using culture data if available.
Historically, management consisted of intravenous antibiotic agents followed by an oral
antibiotic regimen. Evidence has emerged that several oral antibiotic agents have
excellent bioavailability and efficacy similar to that of parental therapy. These oral
antibiotic agents include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones,
linezolid, and metronidazole.20
In the nonsurgical management of hand infections, such as pyogenic flexor
tenosynovitis, a so-called maceration dressing may be considered. The maceration
dressing consists of warm and moist layers of dressings and a heating pad wrapped
around the extremity. This dressing is believed to promote blood flow and antibiotic
delivery and has been shown to decrease hospital length of stay, the duration of
intravenous antibiotic agents before transition to oral antibiotic agents, and the need for
formal irrigation and débridement in the operating room.21
Surgical Management
Surgical wound irrigation is indicated in patients with substantial infectious burden or lack of
response to a trial of antibiotic therapy.
A limited-incision approach may be performed, with closed irrigation of the flexor tendon
sheath intraoperatively and/or postoperatively.

Open approaches are indicated in patients with subcutaneous purulence, necrosis of the
tendon or the pulley system, or digital ischemia.
Age older than 43 years, comorbid diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, renal failure,
subcutaneous purulence, digital ischemia, polymicrobial infection, and delayed management
are poor prognostic factors.

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis who have
substantial infectious burden, who present late (>24 hours of symptoms), or who do not
respond to a trial of antibiotic therapy. Limited-incision approaches over the A1 pulley
and the A5 pulley that allow for closed irrigation of the flexor tendon sheath with the use
of an angiocatheter or a pediatric feeding tube are appropriate in many patients. In
patients with more advanced infection, such as those with subcutaneous purulence,
necrosis of the tendon or the pulley system, or digital ischemia, an open, extensile
approach is more appropriate. A Bruner or midaxial approach can be used for the flexor
tendon sheath.6, 8
Negative prognostic factors for pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis include age older than 43
years, comorbid diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, renal failure,
subcutaneous purulence, digital ischemia, polymicrobial infection, and delayed
management.18, 19 Pang et al18 reported that patients without subcutaneous purulence
and digital ischemia achieved a mean of 80% return of total active motion, patients with
subcutaneous purulence but no digital ischemia achieved a mean of 72% return of total
active motion with an 8% amputation rate, and patients with subcutaneous purulence
and digital ischemia achieved a mean of 49% return of total active motion with a 59%
amputation rate.18

Thenar Space Infection
Thenar space infections are closed space infections superficial to the adductor pollicis, deep to
the index finger flexor tendons, and radial to the midpalmar septum.
The clinical presentation includes swelling of the thenar region, an abducted thumb position,
and pain with thumb opposition.
Incision and drainage via a palmar and/or dorsal approach and antibiotic therapy are the
mainstays of management.
Midpalmar Space Infection
Midpalmar space infections are closed space infections superficial to the third, fourth, and fifth
metacarpals and the volar interossei, deep to the long, ring, and little finger flexor tendons,
radial to the hypothenar septum, and ulnar to the midpalmar septum.
The clinical presentation includes tenderness in the mid-palm, pain with motion of the long
and ring digits, and reversal of normal palmar concavity.

Incision and drainage via a palmar approach and antibiotic therapy are the mainstays of
management.
Hypothenar Space Infection
Hypothenar space infections are closed space infections superficial to the fifth metacarpal and
ulnar to the hypothenar septum.
The clinical presentation includes swelling of the hypothenar region.
Incision and drainage and antibiotic therapy are the mainstays of management.8
Collar Button Infection
Collar button infections are abscesses of the interdigital web spaces spanning volar and dorsal
to the natatory ligaments (Figure 5).
Patients may present with local tenderness, swelling, subcutaneous purulence, and an
abducted position of the digits.
Surgical incision and drainage typically is performed via dual volar and dorsal incisions to
ensure adequate drainage.6

Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infections
Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
Necrotizing soft-tissue infections (NSTIs) are limb-threatening and life-threatening
emergencies.
Type 1 NSTIs are polymicrobial, often caused by aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms.
Type 2 NSTIs are monomicrobial, with group A Streptococcus being the most common
causative microorganism.
Clostridial NSTIs are associated with intravenous drug use (IVDU) and high WBC counts and are
associated with a higher risk for limb loss and death.

Pathoanatomy/Microbiology
NSTIs are limb-threatening and life-threatening emergencies. NSTIs involve the fascia
and subcutaneous tissues and can rapidly spread along fascial planes. The overall
mortality rate of NSTIs is higher than 15%, and the rate of limb loss associated with
extremity NSTIs is higher than 25%.22 Type 1 NSTIs are polymicrobial, often caused by
aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms, frequently in immunocompromised hosts.
Streptococci and Enterobacteriaceae are the most common isolates in patients with a
polymicrobial NSTI. Type 2 NSTIs are monomicrobial, with group A Streptococcus being
the most common causative microorganism.23, 24 Clostridial NSTIs produce local and
systemic toxins and are independently associated with a higher risk for mortality and
limb loss. Clostridial NSTIs should be suspected in patients with IVDU and high WBC
counts.6, 8
Clinical Presentation
The clinical presentation of NSTIs is considerable pain with rapid proximal progression. Other
findings may include induration, crepitus, bullae formation, skin sloughing, skin necrosis, and
sensorimotor changes.
Systematic symptoms of fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status are
common (sepsis).


Clinical Presentation
Initially, NSTIs may present as cellulitis; however, they can rapidly progress proximally.8
Physical examination findings may include tenderness, warmth, erythema, skin
induration, skin sloughing, fluctuance, crepitus, bullae formation, skin necrosis, and
sensorimotor deficits. Systemic symptoms of fever, tachycardia, hypotension and altered
mental status are common (sepsis).24
Diagnostic Studies
Serum laboratory studies, including a complete metabolic panel and a complete blood count,
and blood cultures are helpful.
Radiographs and CT scans are appropriate; however, they should not delay management.

Diagnostic Studies
The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis score aids in distinguishing NSTIs
from non-NSTIs (Table 2). A Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis score of 6
points is associated with a 92% positive predictive value and a 96% negative predictive
value for a NSTI.25

Management
NSTIs are managed surgically by performing prompt débridement of all necrotic tissue and
obtaining surgical cultures. Repeat débridement procedures are performed at 24- to 48-hour

intervals until the infection is controlled.
Limb amputation may be lifesaving in patients in extremis who are critically ill.
Negative prognostic factors for NSTIs include advanced age, medical comorbidities, elevated
WBC count, elevated creatinine level, hypotension, and delayed surgical management.
Clostridial NSTIs are independently associated with a four-fold higher risk of limb amputation
and mortality.

Management
NSTIs are surgically managed via prompt aggressive débridement of the infected and
necrotic tissues. Intraoperatively, the subcutaneous fat and fascia may appear liquefied,
with a dishwater fluid appearance; malodor is common. Extensive débridement is
performed, and cultures are obtained. The wounds are left open, and débridement is
repeated every 24 to 48 hours until the infection is controlled (Figure 6). Limb
amputation may be necessary for prompt control of the infection and sepsis and may be
lifesaving in patients in extremis who are critically ill. Patients with a NSTI often benefit
from intensive care and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic agents, which can be
empiric based on common organisms and then tailored based on surgical culture data.6,
8
Negative prognostic factors for NSTIs include older age, two or more associated
comorbidities, delayed débridement (>24 hours),24 a WBC count higher than 30,000
cells/μL, creatinine level higher than 2 mg/dL, and heart disease. These factors are
independent predictors of mortality. A systolic blood pressure lower than 90 mm Hg and
heart disease on presentation 16 are independent predictors of limb amputation.
Clostridial NSTIs are independently associated with a four-fold higher risk of limb
amputation and mortality.22

IVDU-Associated Infections
Epidemiology/Microbiology
As many as 20% of acute hand infections are associated with IVDU.
Most IVDU-related upper extremity infections are caused by Streptococcus.

Epidemiology/Microbiology
Substance abuse is a national health epidemic. Approximately 17% of patients who
undergo hand and upper extremity surgery report chronic opioid use. Approximately
20% of acute hand infections are related to IVDU.26 Most IVDU-related upper extremity
infections are caused by Streptococcus, followed by S aureus, E corrodens, and
anaerobes.27
Risk Factors
Patients with IVDU-associated infections of the upper extremity are more likely to have
comorbid psychiatric conditions, HIV infection, and hepatitis C virus infection.

Risk Factors
Individuals with an IVDU disorder are a vulnerable patient population. Nearly one-third
of patients with an IVDU disorder are uninsured, and these patients are more likely to
have psychiatric comorbidities, HIV infection, and hepatitis C virus infection. IVDU-
associated infections of the upper extremity more often are polymicrobial in etiology,
and patients with an IVDU-associated infection are almost three times more likely to
require surgical treatment than patients without an IVDU-associated infection. Typically,
patients with an IVDU-associated infection require longer inpatient hospital stays and
have a higher risk of eloping against medical advice.27, 28, 29
Diagnostic Studies
Serum laboratory studies, including a WBC count, ESR, and CRP level and blood cultures are
necessary.
Radiographs are obtained to assess for osteomyelitis, gas formation, and retained foreign
bodies.

Sporotrichosis
Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis presents as a chain of nontender, firm subcutaneous
nodules with ulceration.
Caused by Sporothrix schenckii, farmers, gardeners, and florists are at risk for this infection.
The diagnosis is established via a swab or tissue fungal culture.
The preferred treatment option is itraconazole.

Sporotrichosis
Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is the most common subcutaneous fungal infection in
the hand and is caused by S schenckii. This fungus resides in soil and on plants. Florists,
gardeners, and farmers are at particular risk for this disease because spores can be
inoculated through a break in the dermis. Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis typically
begins as a painless pink papule and evolves to an ulceration. A chain of subcutaneous
nodules that are firm, mobile, and potentially ulcerative can develop. The diagnosis is
established via fungal cultures of ulcer swabs or tissue biopsies. The mainstay of
management is the oral antifungal medication itraconazole.31, 32, 33
Aspergillosis
Aspergillosis of the hand is a rare fungal infection observed in immunocompromised patients.
Caused by Aspergillus flavus, this infection can be introduced through intravenous access.
Primary aspergillosis of the hand presents as ulceration and necrosis beginning at the site of
intravenous access.
The diagnosis is established via tissue fungal culture. A flavus characteristically has
dichotomously branched septate hyphae observed on microscopic images.
The preferred treatment option is systemic antifungal medication and surgical débridement of
local necrotic tissues.
Hematogenous dissemination and death are common.34, 35

Mucormycosis of the hand is a rare fungal infection caused by the Mucoromycotina group of
fungi and is predominately observed in immunocompromised patients.
Risk factors for mucormycosis include contaminated traumatic wounds, burns, IVDU,
hematologic malignancy, diabetic ketoacidosis, and chronic corticosteroid use.
The clinical presentation includes ulceration and local tissue necrosis (Figure 9).
The diagnosis is established via tissue fungal culture. On histologic analysis, mucormycosis
exhibits non-septate hyphae with 90° branching and vascular invasion with small vessel
thrombosis.
The preferred treatment option is systemic antifungal medication and surgical débridement of
local necrotic tissues. Limb amputation is common.36

Mycobacterium Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis of the hand is a rare mycobacterial infection that can manifest in the skin,
tenosynovial tissues, bones, or joints (Figure 10). 
The diagnosis is established via acid-fast bacteria tissue cultures, which often require weeks to
months to grow because of the paucibacillary nature of this infection.37
Management involves a multidrug regimen, typically consisting of isoniazid, rifampin,
pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
Mycobacterium Marinum
Mycobacterium marinum is the most common atypical mycobacterial infection of the hand.
Risk factors include exposure to marine environments, and patients may report a puncture
wound followed by digital swelling and stiffness.
Management involves anti-tuberculous medications and synovectomy for tenosynovial
disease.38

Orf
An orf is a parapoxvirus infection of human hands obtained via contact with sheep or goats.
The typical clinical course involves a papular lesion at the site of inoculation followed by an
outer halo, after which drying and spontaneous resolution occur.
Herpetic Whitlow
Herpetic whitlow is a herpes simplex virus infection of the hand and classically involves the
thumb, index finger, and long finger of the dominant hand of healthcare workers.
Lesions are characterized by painful vesicles with an erythematous base, which can spread
and become turbid and hemorrhagic over the course of weeks.
Mistaking the clear vesicular fluid for purulence may lead to unnecessary débridement,
increasing the risk for bacterial superinfection.
Complete resolution of herpetic whitlow occurs within 3 weeks, and surgical management is
contraindicated.
Oral antiviral medications may be beneficial in limiting the clinical course of protracted cases,
decreasing recurrences, and aborting a recurrent case in the prodromal phase.

Herpetic Whitlow
Herpetic whitlow is a herpes simplex virus infection of the hand. The mechanism of
exposure typically occurs via contact with a mucous membrane; therefore, herpetic
whitlow commonly is observed in the thumb, index finger, and long finger of the
dominant hand of healthcare workers.38 Digital symptoms may be preceded by a flu-like
prodrome. Subsequent to an incubation period of 2 to 20 days after inoculation, an early
herpetic whitlow lesion typically presents as throbbing pain and vesicle formation in the
fingertip. Dissimilar to a felon, the pulp space generally is not tense. The lesion is most
contagious during the first 12 days during which the virus sheds. After this period, pain
subsides and the clear vesicle becomes turbid or hemorrhagic. Complete resolution of
herpetic whitlow occurs within 3 weeks. A diagnosis of herpetic whitlow can be
established via a patient history and physical examination alone; however, additional
confirmatory tests include a Tzanck smear and a viral culture of the vesicular fluid.
Management of active herpetic whitlow includes analgesic agents and dressings to

Mimickers of Infection
Gout and Pseudogout
Gout is a crystalline arthropathy of monosodium urate monohydrate crystal deposition.
Gouty flares of the distal interphalangeal joints can mimic felon, paronychia, and distal
interphalangeal joint septic arthritis.
Acute gout flares are managed via fluid resuscitation, avoidance of precipitating factors,
NSAIDs, oral or intra-articular glucocorticoids, colchicine, and interleukin-1 inhibitors.
Pseudogout is a crystalline arthropathy of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition.

Gout and Pseudogout
Acute gout flares are characterized by pain and swelling, and 12% to 35% of patients
who have gout present with tophi. A patient’s WBC count, ESR, and CRP level may be
elevated in the diagnostic workup. Although a serum uric acid level often is ordered, it
usually is normal. Therefore, an elevated serum uric acid level may aid in the diagnosis
of gout; however, a normal serum uric acid level does not exclude gout. If the joint is
aspirated, crystal analysis may be performed. The causative agent of the clinical
condition of gout, which is monosodium urate monohydrate crystals, characteristically
appear negatively birefringent on polarized light microscopic images. Acute gout flares
are managed via fluid resuscitation; avoidance of precipitating factors, such as alcohol,
diuretics, and certain foods (purine-rich foods, such as seafood/shellfish, red meat,

Acute pseudogout flares are characterized by pain and swelling, and a patient’s WBC
count, ESR, and CRP level may be elevated. Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals
characteristically appear positively birefringent on polarized light microscopic images.
Acute pseudogout flares are managed via NSAIDs and oral or intra-articular
glucocorticoids.41
Calcific Tendinitis/Periarticulitis
Calcific tendinitis/periarticulitis results from calcium hydroxyapatite deposition in the tendons,
ligaments, or capsule about a joint.
Acute flares about the distal interphalangeal joints may present as pain, swelling, and
erythema and can mimic felon, paronychia, and distal interphalangeal joint septic arthritis.
Calcific tendinitis/periarticulitis is distinguished from these infectious processes by the
characteristic calcific deposition in the inflamed region.
The natural history is self-limiting, and management consists of NSAIDs.
Neoplastic Disorders
Numerous malignancies may mimic fingertip infections, including melanoma, squamous cell
carcinoma, papillary adenocarcinoma, and Kaposi sarcoma.43
In addition, acrometastatic disease may mimic a soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, or
tenosynovitis. The most common primary malignancies that metastasize to the hands are lung,
gastrointestinal, kidney, and breast cancers.44, 45
Chronic immunosuppression and chronic, isolated, nonhealing paronychia should increase
suspicion for malignancy, and biopsy should be considered.43

Pyoderma gangrenosum is an immune-mediated disorder characterized by sterile pustules
with surrounding erythema followed by ulceration with central necrosis and a well-demarcated
border.
The management of pyoderma gangrenosum consists of local wound care and systemic
medical management, such as that via corticosteroids or other immunosuppressant agents.
Surgical treatment is contraindicated in patients with active pyoderma gangrenosum because
it evokes a pathergic response and worsens the condition.

Pyoderma Gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is an immune-mediated disorder that can involve the trunk or
extremities, including the hand. Pyoderma gangrenosum is preceded by minor trauma in
30% of patients. Pyoderma gangrenosum is clinically painful and may be accompanied
by a fever and malaise. Pyoderma gangrenosum is associated with a systemic
autoimmune disorder in 50% to 70% of patients, most frequently inflammatory bowel
disease. Active pyoderma gangrenosum is characterized by sterile pustules with
surrounding erythema followed by ulceration with central necrosis and a well-
demarcated border. Cultures are sterile in patients with pyoderma gangrenosum, and
tissue biopsy is performed to rule out malignancy and reveals lymphocytic infiltration in
patients in the early stages followed by neutrophilic infiltration and hemorrhage in
patients in the later stages. The management of pyoderma gangrenosum consists of
local wound care and systemic medical management, such as that via corticosteroids or
other immunosuppressant agents. Surgical treatment is contraindicated in patients with
active pyoderma gangrenosum because it evokes a pathergic response and worsens the
condition.46
